The results of this analysis for the southeastern region of Montana are presented in Table II-4. Local high winds associated with thunderstorm activity are not uncommon in spring and summer.

Hailstorms are typically the most common and damaging form of severe weather in Montana. Limited mainly to July and August, hailstorms cause crop and property damage amounting to about $5 million annually (Cordell, 1971).
Floods are most likely to occur in spring and early summer as a result of melting snow. Such flooding is compounded when general, heavy rains fall on the snowpack. Floods in the streambeds of the Sarpy Creek area, however, are more likely to be the result of locally heavy thundershowers in late spring and summer.
